units.la: Sisto tibi tandem, bene-vole Lector! elegantissi-mam hanc Introductionem in Historiam universalem, quæ, cùm ob precium suum, quo habui, in scrinio meo hactenus latitaverit, ob maximum usum, qui etiam visus est celeberrimis Viris, quibus copiam ejus feci, diutius Tibi de-esse haud debuit.
units.tr: At last I present to you, kind reader, this most elegant Introduction to Universal History. Because I had bought it at a high price, it has lain hidden in my chest until now, but given its very great usefulness, which has also been evident to the most celebrated men to whom I gave access to it, it should not have been kept from you any longer.

units.la: Quàm enim necessaria sit Summaria quædam notitia vastum Historiæ Universalis studium feliciter aggressuro, post Polybium Insignem Historicum, constans doctorum testatur autoritas. Cumq; notitia hæc varie à variis qvæsita & comparata fuerit, in hâc Introductione Clarissimus Autor, præter ab aliis observatam temporis rationem, loci qvoqve diversitatem probè consideravit, & cujuscunq; Imperii fata seorsim, eorumqve connexionis dispersusqve causas summô studiô docuit, ut Libellus iste non Tyronibus modò in historicis, sed profectioribus pariter emolumento esse, optimôq; Jure Introductio æqvè ac Memorialis Liber dici possit. Et qvis de accuratâ ejus ac nervosâ elaboratione dubitabit, nisi qvem fugit gratia, qvam Orbis ejus Politicus atqve Im-perans perans, Historia quoq; Universalis, Arca Noë inscripta, apud Orbem Literarium hactenus habuit; quodque Autor laborem illum præsenti limâ persecutus fuerit.
units.tr: How necessary a certain summary knowledge is to one about to undertake the vast study of universal history with success is attested by the agreed authority of learned men, going back to Polybius, the distinguished historian. Since this knowledge has been sought and compiled in various ways by various people, the most distinguished author, in this Introduction, has carefully considered not only the order of time, which others have observed, but also the diversity of places. He has taught with the greatest care the fortunes of each empire separately, and the causes of their connection and dispersal. So this little book can be of use not only to beginners in history but equally to the more advanced, and it may rightly be called an Introduction and a Memorial Book alike. Who will doubt its careful and vigorous workmanship, unless he has missed the favour which the author's Orbis Politicus and Orbis Imperans, and his Universal History entitled Arca Noë, have so far enjoyed in the literary world? And the author has now polished that work with the present file.

units.la: Ne tamen habeas quod amplius in opusculo hoc desiderare, possis, menda, quibus scatuit Manuscriptum prius à me visum, passim expunxi, & quantum in me fuit, correctum tibi adque præsens tempus continuatum offero exemplar, cui simul summaria, nec non Index opusculi Tabula quoq;, omnem Introductionem uno quasi intuitu repræsentans, adjecta sunt. Utere his feliciter & vale.
units.tr: So that you may have nothing further to wish for in this little work, I have struck out, wherever I found them, the errors with which the manuscript I saw earlier was full. As far as I was able, I offer you a corrected copy, brought up to the present time, to which summaries have been added, together with an index of the little work and a table presenting the whole Introduction at a single glance. Use them to your advantage, and farewell.

units.la: Ne vacua relinquatur hæc pagina, Typographo lubuit apponere impressa Autoris scripta maximè hactenus cognita. Sunt autem I. Dissertationes Historicæ & Politicæ. II. Historiæ Ecclesiasticæ & Civilis Compendium. III. Orbis Politicus Imperiorum, Regnorum, Principatuum & Rerumpublicarum; cum Memorabilibus Historicis, & Geographiâ Veteri ac Recenti. IV. Orbis Imperans, in tredecim maxima Imperia divisus. V. Arca Noæ, sive Historia Imperiorum & regnorum, à condito Orbe ad nostra tempora. VI. Arca Mosis, sive Historia Mundi, quæ complectitur primordia rerum Naturalium, omniumq; artium ac Scientiarum.
units.tr: So that this page is not left blank, the printer has chosen to add the author's published writings that are best known so far. They are: I. Historical and Political Dissertations. II. A Compendium of Ecclesiastical and Civil History. III. Orbis Politicus, of Empires, Kingdoms, Principalities and Commonwealths; with Historical Memorabilia, and Ancient and Modern Geography. IV. Orbis Imperans, divided into thirteen very great empires. V. Arca Noë, or a History of Empires and Kingdoms, from the founding of the world to our own times. VI. Arca Mosis, or a History of the World, which embraces the beginnings of natural things and of all arts and sciences.

units.tr: Tabu'a: representing the Introduction to Universal History at one glance.

units.la: HIstoria universalis tradit Imperiorum omnis ævi res maximas,
units.tr: Universal history sets forth the greatest deeds of the empires of every age.

units.la: Historia est vel Universalis vel Particularis.
units.tr: History is either universal or particular.

units.la: Universalis complectitur maximas Imperiorum Res ab Orbe condito, secundum certam temporum seriem, ad nostram usq; ætatem.
units.tr: Universal history embraces the greatest deeds of empires from the creation of the world, in a fixed chronological sequence, down to our own age.

units.la: Particularis singularum gentium nationumq;, vel alicujus tantùm ævi res complectitur.
units.tr: Particular history embraces the deeds of individual peoples and nations, or of some one age only.
It is either before the Flood or after the Flood.
Before the Flood nothing is known except what Moses records.

units.la: Imperium unum commemoratur fundatum à Kaino, cujus regia sedes fuit Urbs Hanoch; Sed incertum est, in qua regione sita, ubi septem ordine Reges, ejus posteri, regnârunt; ut Augustinus tradit.
units.tr: One empire is recorded, founded by Cain, whose royal seat was the city Hanoch. But it is uncertain in what region it lay, where seven kings, his descendants, reigned in order, as Augustine reports.

units.la: Quod verò Abydenus & Apollodorus aliud quoddam regnum Chaldæorum, ejusque Reges ab Aloro ad Xisuthrum sive Noachum referunt, fabulosum est.
units.tr: As for Abydenus and Apollodorus, who relate some other kingdom of the Chaldeans, and its kings from Alorus down to Xisuthrus, or Noah, that is fabulous.
After the Flood history is either ancient or recent.

units.la: Per antiquam intelligimus res illorum Imperiorum, quorum memoria & nomen penitùs extinctum est, ut: Assyriorum Lacedæmoniorum, &c. Per Novam, illa, quæ hodie per universum orbem florent, Imperia.
units.tr: By ancient we understand the affairs of those empires whose memory and name have been utterly extinguished, such as the Assyrian, the Lacedaemonian, and so on. By recent we understand those empires which today flourish throughout the whole world.

units.la: Antiqua est vel Asiatica, Africana, Europæa.
units.tr: Ancient history is either Asiatic, African, or European.

units.la: Asiatica est vel Babylonica, Persica, Scythica, Indica.
units.tr: Asiatic history is either Babylonian, Persian, Scythian, or Indian.

units.la: Imperium Babylonicum {t}à Chaldæis ad Arabes, ab hisad Assyrios pervenit.
units.tr: The Babylonian empire passed from the Chaldeans to the Arabs, and from them to the Assyrians.

units.la: Conditum est à Nimrodo A. M. 1787. Post Nimrodum defecit Regum feries, usq; ad A.M. 2242. Tum enim Evechous qui aliis Jupiter Belus, natione Chaldæus, regnare cæpit. Ejus familia extincta fuit ab A-rabibus, quorum Rex Mardocentes Babyloniam occupavit. Hujus po-steritatem Regnô exuit A. M. 2682. Belus Assyrius, cujus filius fuit fa-mosus ille Ninus, à quo Profani Historiarum Scriptores initium faciunt. Sed male hunc Ninum ad antiquissi-ma tempora referunt, & proximum à Nimrodo faciunt: qui error universam Chronologiam pudendis erroribus implevit. Nam vulgò ab hoc Nino usq; ad Sardanapalum 1300. annos effluxisse tradunt. At verò constat ex Herodoto, ab hoc Nino usque ad Sardanapalum non nisi 520. numerari. Ergò totis 800. annis erratum fuit circa ætatem Nini.
units.tr: It was founded by Nimrod in A.M. 1787. After Nimrod the succession of kings fails, until A.M. 2242. For then Evechous, who is called Jupiter Belus by others, a Chaldean by nation, began to reign. His family was wiped out by the Arabs, whose king Mardocentes seized Babylon. His posterity was stripped of the kingdom in A.M. 2682. Then came Belus the Assyrian, whose son was the famous Ninus, from whom the profane writers of history make their beginning. But they wrongly place this Ninus in the most ancient times and make him the next after Nimrod, and this error has filled the whole of chronology with shameful mistakes. For it is commonly reported that 1300 years elapsed from this Ninus to Sardanapalus. Yet it is clear from Herodotus that only 520 years are counted from this Ninus to Sardanapalus. Therefore the dating of Ninus was wrong by a full 800 years.

units.la: Huic Nino maximæ res atq; amplissimæ adscribuntur, quod Imperiū ab India usq; ad Hellespontum propagauerit & totius Asiæ (Indis atqve Scythis exceptis) Imperator fuerit: qvod & fabulosum est. Nam testatur Dionysius Halicarnassæus antiqvis-simos illos Assyriorum Reges non nisi exiguam qvandam Asiæ partem obtinuisse. Dionys. in proœmio.
units.tr: Very great and famous achievements are ascribed to this Ninus: that he extended his empire from India to the Hellespont and was emperor of all Asia (except India and Scythia). This too is fabulous. For Dionysius of Halicarnassus testifies that those most ancient kings of the Assyrians held only a small part of Asia. Dionysius, in the preface.

units.la: Nino successit Semiramis, virago illa atq; Amazon, cujus & res magnâ ex parte fabulosæ. Post Semiramidem regnasse dicitur Ninyas, & alii longâ serie, quorum non nisi nomina extant, & ea fabulis polluta. vid. Chronolog. Alstedii.
units.tr: Ninus was succeeded by Semiramis, that virago and Amazon, whose deeds are for the most part fabulous too. After Semiramis Ninyas is said to have reigned, and others in a long line, of whom only the names survive, and these tainted with fables. See Alstedius's Chronology.

units.la: Primus autem Assyriorum Rex, cujus potentia in exteris magna, fuit Phul Assur, cujus literæ Sacræ mentionem faciunt 2. Reg. 15. & seqq. 1. Paral.[?] 28.
units.tr: The first king of the Assyrians whose power abroad was great was Phul Assur, whom the sacred letters mention at 2 Kings 15 and following, and 1 Paral. 28.

units.la: Hujus vel Filius vel Nepos Sardanapalus censetur, sub quo Imperium Assyriorum convulsum fuit.
units.tr: His son or grandson is considered to be Sardanapalus, under whom the empire of the Assyrians was overthrown.

units.la: Divisum est in Mediam, Babyloniam, Assyriam, Explicatio 1.

Causa divisionis fuit Sardana-pali effœminata mollities, quam dedignati Arbaces Medorum, & Belochus (Belesis) Babyloniorum Praefecti, rebellarunt, ac Ninive expugnata, cum se incendio confumsifset Sardanapalus, Imperium in tres partes, Mediam, Babyloniam & Assyriam, diviserunt.
units.tr: The cause of the division was the effeminate softness of Sardanapalus, which the governors Arbaces of the Medes and Belochus (Belesis) of the Babylonians disdained, and so they revolted. When Nineveh had been taken and Sardanapalus had burned himself to death, they divided the empire into three parts: Media, Babylonia and Assyria.

units.la: Medorum Rex factus fuit Arbaces, sed paulo post regno sese abdicavit ac Medis libertatem reddidit.
units.tr: Arbaces was made king of the Medes, but a little later he gave up the kingdom and returned freedom to the Medes.

units.la: Carucrunt igitur Regibus usq; ad Dejicen, qvi magna illam urbem Ecbatanam condidit. Hunc exceperunt Phraortes, Cyaxares, & ultimus omnium Astyages, cui regnum Cyrus ademit.
units.tr: So there were kings down to Deioces, who founded the great city Ecbatana. He was succeeded by Phraortes and Cyaxares, and last of all by Astyages, from whom Cyrus took the kingdom.

units.la: Regnum Assyria obtinuit Tiglath Pileser, Æliano Thilgamus, Casto-ri Rhodio Ninus junior dictus: cui successerunt Salmanassar, Sennache-rib, Assarhaddon, Soasduchinus & Chynaladanus sive Saracus, sub qvo Ninive a Medis & Babyloniis exci-sa fuit.
units.tr: Assyria was held by Tiglath Pileser, called Thilgamus by Aelian and Ninus the Younger by Castor of Rhodes. He was succeeded by Shalmaneser, Sennacherib, Esarhaddon, Soasduchinus and Chynaladanus, or Saracus, under whom Nineveh was destroyed by the Medes and Babylonians.

units.la: Babyloniam sortitus fuit Belesis fi-ve Baladan, qvi & Nabonassarus di-citur celeberrimus apud Ptolemaum & alios antiqvos Scriptores, propter peculiarem æram sive temporum E-pocham, qvæ ab ipso Æra Nabo-nassari appellatur. Post qvem varii Reges, sed celebriores Marodach sive Mardochembadus, ab ipso Ptolemæo memoratus.
units.tr: Babylonia fell to Belesis, or Baladan, who is also called Nabonassar, most famous among Ptolemy and other ancient writers because of the distinct era or epoch of time, which is named the Era of Nabonassar after him. After him there were various kings, but the more famous was Marodach, or Mardokempadus, mentioned by Ptolemy himself.
Nebuchadnezzar made the Babylonian empire the greatest of all.

units.la: Unde initium Monarchiæ Babylo-niorum jure meritoq; collocatur in hoc Nebucadnezare, de quo ipse Deus apud Daniel dicit, quod ipsi tradiderit omnia regna mundi. Hujus opera fuerunt Mœnia Babylonica; & quæ Historici vulgo adscribunt Nino, ea de hoc Nebucadnezare intelligenda sunt; Sic historiæ Semiramidis ad Uxorem ejus Nitocrin spectant. Post Nebucadnezarem regnarunt Evilmerodach & alii quidam, quorum breve fuit imperium. Ultimus fuit Belsazar, sub quo Cyrus Persarum Rex Babyloniam ex-pupugnavit, & Dário Medo tradi-dit.
units.tr: Hence the beginning of the Babylonian monarchy is rightly and deservedly placed in this Nebuchadnezzar, of whom God himself says in Daniel that he gave him all the kingdoms of the world. The Babylonian walls were his work, and what historians commonly ascribe to Ninus must be understood of this Nebuchadnezzar. Likewise the stories of Semiramis refer to his wife Nitocris. After Nebuchadnezzar, Evil-Merodach and some others reigned, whose rule was brief. The last was Belshazzar, under whom Cyrus, king of the Persians, stormed Babylon and handed it over to Darius the Mede.

units.la: De mirabili nativitate & educatione Cyri legantur Herodotus & Justinus; is[?] origine Persa Imperium Babylonicum destruxit, & summam potestatem ad Persas transtulit, circa Annum M. 3468. Longe autem amplior Monarchia Persica, quàm Babylonica fuit; quippe complexa totam Asiam, solâ Indiâ & Scythiâ exceptis.
units.tr: On the wonderful birth and upbringing of Cyrus read Herodotus and Justin. Being a Persian by origin, he destroyed the Babylonian empire and transferred supreme power to the Persians, around the year 3468 of the world. The Persian monarchy was far larger than the Babylonian, for it embraced all of Asia, except India and Scythia alone.

units.la: Cyro successit filius Cambyses, qui Ægyptum debellavit.
units.tr: Cyrus was succeeded by his son Cambyses, who subdued Egypt.

units.la: Cùm post Cambysis obitum Magi, subornato quodam falsario, occupassent Imperium, redetectâ VII. nobilissimi Persarum proceres contra ipsum conjurarunt, & obtruncato tô illô deceptore Darium Hystaspis filium Regem salutarunt. Cui successit Xerxes, sub quo Imperium Persicum omnium magnificentissimum fuit. Post hunc regnarunt Artaxerxes, Ochus, Arses sive Arsames & ultimus Darius Codomannus; quo triplici prælio superato Alexander Magnus imperio potitus fuit.
units.tr: After the death of Cambyses the Magi, having set up a certain impostor, seized the empire; but the seven most noble Persian nobles discovered the deception, conspired against him, cut down that deceiver, and hailed Darius Hystaspis as king. He was succeeded by Xerxes, under whom the Persian empire was at its most magnificent. After him Artaxerxes, Ochus, Arses or Arsames reigned, and last Darius Codomannus. After three battles with him had been won, Alexander the Great gained the empire.

units.la: Varia Scytharum regna fuerunt: Præcipua autem Getarum, Tauricanorum, Amazonum, Sacarum, Massagetarum vel Neurorum, Agathyrsorum, Gelonorum, Budinorum, Sarmatarum & Celtarum: Sed hæc omnia parum nobis cognita sunt. Celeberrimi inter Scythas fuere Europæi ad Danubium atq; Tanaim, & Asiatici sive Massagetæ, quorum Regina fuit Tomyris, quæ Cyrum in prælio obtruncavit.
units.tr: There were various Scythian kingdoms. The chief were those of the Getae, Tauricans, Amazons, Sacae, Massagetae or Neuri, Agathyrsi, Geloni, Budini, Sarmatians and Celts. But all of these are little known to us. The most famous among the Scythians were the European ones by the Danube and the Tanais, and the Asiatic ones, that is the Massagetae, whose queen was Tomyris, who cut down Cyrus in battle.

units.la: Inter omnes autem Scytharum res antiquas memorabilis imprimis est ipsorum expeditio Asiatica, quâ Rege Madye sive Indathyrso ingenti cum exercitu universam penè Asiam, usq; ad Ægyptum, Imperio suo subjecerunt, & per 28. annos obtinuerunt; de quo Herodotus lib. 1. & 4.
units.tr: Among all the ancient events of the Scythians, the most memorable is their Asiatic expedition, in which, under king Madyes or Indathyrsus, with a huge army they brought almost all of Asia, as far as Egypt, under their rule and held it for 28 years. On this see Herodotus, books 1 and 4.

units.la: In hac expeditione Scythæ Bactrianis & Parthis originem dederunt: quippe Scytharum pars reliqua in Persia & Media tandem in Parthorum & Bactrianorum prævalidas nationes excreverunt.
units.tr: In this expedition the Scythians gave rise to the Bactrians and Parthians, for the remaining part of the Scythians, in Persia and Media, at last grew into the very powerful nations of the Parthians and Bactrians.
India was divided into several kingdoms.

units.la: Indorum Imperium conditum traditur a Baccho, quicunq; tandem is fuerit; post quem 153. ordine reges regnasse tradunt, quorum nec quidem nomina nota sunt. Mentio unius tantum fit Regis Stawrobatos [?], qui bellum contra Semiramidem gessisse dicitur. India igitur incognignita fere mansit ad tempora Ale-xandri M. cujus ætate XII. Indorum regna numerabantur ex quibus præ-cipua fuerunt Taxiles & Pori.
units.tr: The empire of the Indians is said to have been founded by Bacchus, whoever he may have been; after him, it is recorded, 153 kings reigned in succession, whose names are not even known. Only one is mentioned, King Stawrobates [?], who is said to have waged war against Semiramis. India therefore remained almost unknown until the time of Alexander the Great, in whose age twelve kingdoms of the Indians were counted, of which the chief were those of Taxiles and Porus.
The Egyptians, having taken possession of Asia, founded the Chinese kingdom.

units.la: Celeberrimum in antiqua hi-storia regnum Ægyptiorum fuit; Sed catalogus Regum, qui vulgò extat, admodum corruptus & inexplicabilis est.
units.tr: The kingdom of the Egyptians was the most famous in ancient history; but the catalogue of kings that is commonly extant is very corrupt and unintelligible.

units.la: Imperium Ægyptiorum, quod in universam penè Asiam obtinuerunt, apud Historicos parùm celebratur: extat autem ejus perpraeclara mentio apud Herodotum; sed in primis apud Tacitum l.2, Annal.c.60. qui locus admodum memorabilis ac notatū dignus est.
units.tr: The empire of the Egyptians, which they held over nearly all of Asia, is little celebrated by the historians. A most distinguished mention of it is found in Herodotus, but especially in Tacitus, Annal.c.60. book 2, a passage that is very memorable and worth noting.

units.la: Quando autem & sub quibus regibus Asia potiti sint, non consentiunt Historici: quippe Herodotus Sesostrim, Tacitus Rhamsem vocat. Maxime probabile est ex Sacris Literis, tunc temporis Aegyptios expugnasse Asiam, cum Sisac qui videtur esse Sesostris, Hierosolymam expugnasset, & cum innumerabili exercitu expeditione suscepisset: quod factum est, cum regnaret Rehabeam; de quo 1. Reg. 14. v.25. & 2. Chron.12 2.
units.tr: Historians do not agree on when, or under which kings, they gained possession of Asia: Herodotus calls the king Sesostris, Tacitus calls him Rhamses. It is most probable from Sacred Letters that the Egyptians conquered Asia at the time when Sisac, who seems to be Sesostris, had captured Jerusalem and undertaken the expedition with an innumerable army. This happened when Rehabeam was reigning; see 1 Reg. 14. v.25. and 2 Chron. 12. v.2.

units.la: In hac expeditione conditum ab Aegyptiis Sinense Imperium admodum probabile videtur. Est enim maxima convenientia inter antiquos Aegyptios & hodiernos Sinenses. Et Ja[?] Jesuita Martinus Martinius, qvi nu-per ex Sina ad nos rediit, in eâdem est sententia, Sinensium nationem atq; Rempubl. ab Ægyptiis esse prose-ctam.
units.tr: It seems quite probable that the Chinese Empire was founded by the Egyptians on this expedition. For there is a very great resemblance between the ancient Egyptians and the present-day Chinese. The Jesuit Martinus Martinius, who lately returned to us from China, is of the same opinion, that the Chinese nation and commonwealth were derived from the Egyptians.

units.la: Æthiopes amplissimum per Africam & Arabiam Imperium condiderunt.
units.tr: The Ethiopians founded a very extensive empire across Africa and Arabia.

units.la: Qvod & parùm à Scriptoribus celebratur. Mentio ejus fit in sacra Scriptura 2. Chron. 14. ubi Serah Æthiops cum innumerabili exercitu deletus dicitur. Postea alius quidam Æthiops cum innumerabili exercitu, cujus nomen fuit Thirhaka, Africam fere totam obtinuit, cujus mentio fit 2. Reg. 19, & Esaiæ 37. v. 9. Hunc Strabo l. 1. & 15. vocat Temo-nem, & maximis Imperatoribus prisci ævi adscribit, atq; etiam superatis Herculeis columnis Europæ victri-cia arma intulisse vult.
units.tr: This is not much celebrated by the writers. Mention of it is made in holy Scripture, 2 Chron. 14, where Zerah the Ethiopian is said to have been destroyed with an innumerable army. Afterwards another Ethiopian, with an innumerable army, whose name was Tirhakah, gained possession of almost all of Africa; his mention is made in 2 Kings 19 and Isaiah 37:9. Strabo, books 1 and 15, calls him Temon, and ascribes him to the greatest commanders of ancient times, and even wants him to have carried his victorious arms into Europe, beyond the Pillars of Hercules.

units.la: Gracia initio inter varios reges divisa fuit.
units.tr: Greece was at first divided among various kings.

units.la: Inter præcipua & antiquissima Græcorum Regna hæc fuerunt: Sicyoniorum, Argivorum, Spartanorum, Messeniorum, Ariarathum, Atheniensium, Thebanorum, Thessalorum.
units.tr: Among the chief and most ancient Greek kingdoms were these: those of the Sicyonians, Argives, Spartans, Messenians, Ariarathes, Athenians, Thebans, and Thessalians.

units.la: Novam regum Dynastiam per GræGræciam sive Peloponnesum, condiderunt Heraclidæ, sive posteri Herculis: Sed omnia in Historia Græcâ incerta & fabulosa, usq; ad initia Olympiadum.
units.tr: The Heraclidae, that is, the descendants of Hercules, established a new dynasty of kings throughout Greece, or the Peloponnese; but everything in Greek history up to the beginning of the Olympiads is uncertain and fabulous.
The Greeks abolished the kingdoms and set up republics.

units.la: Ex tot regnis duo tantum remanserunt, Spartanum & Macedonicum: reliqua omnia in liberas respublicas transmutata fuerunt.
units.tr: Of so many kingdoms, only two remained, the Spartan and the Macedonian; all the rest were changed into free republics.

units.la: Philippus Rex Macedoniæ universam Græciam in unum iterum corpus redegit.
units.tr: Philip, King of Macedonia, brought all Greece once more into one body.

units.la: Hujus Philippi maximæ fuerunt res, & ipse fundamenta jecit ejus Imperii, quod paulò post Alexan-der M.[?] constituit. Cùm igitur videret Philippus Græciam in tot Respubl. divisam perpetuis laborare dissensionibus domesticis, ipse vi armorum Dominum totius Græciæ se constituit, & Corinthi Dux omnium Græcorum est proclamatus.
units.tr: The deeds of this Philip were very great, and he laid the foundations of that empire which Alexander the Great established shortly afterwards. Since Philip saw that Greece, divided into so many republics, was labouring under constant domestic dissensions, he made himself, by force of arms, lord of all Greece, and was proclaimed leader of all the Greeks at Corinth.
Alexander the Great founded a very vast empire.

units.la: Cùm Philippus cunctas Græcorum nationes sub unum iterum Imperium redegisset, Filius ipsius Alexander M. suscepta expeditione Asiatica, Darium Codomannum Persarum Imperatorem debellavit, & Imperiô usq; in Indiam propagato omnium maximam, quæ unquam fuerunt, Monarchiam condidit, & Scythis tantùm in Asia, Romanis in Europa, Carthaginiensibus in Africa exceptis, reliqua omnia Imperia & Regna suo dominio subjecit.
units.tr: After Philip had once more brought all the Greek nations under one empire, his son Alexander the Great undertook the Asiatic expedition, defeated Darius Codomannus, king of the Persians, and, extending his rule as far as India, founded the greatest monarchy that has ever existed. Apart from the Scythians in Asia, the Romans in Europe and the Carthaginians in Africa, he brought all the remaining empires and kingdoms under his dominion.

units.la: Imperium Macedonicum in Asiam, Thraciam, Macedoniam, Syriam & Ægyptum dividitur.
units.tr: The Macedonian empire is divided into Asia, Thrace, Macedonia, Syria and Egypt.

units.la: Causa fuit divisionis ambigua illa Alexandri moribundi vox: qui interrogatus quemnam successorem relinqueret, respondit: dignissimum. Unde quanquam & Fratrem & duos Filios & Filiam haberet, tamen quod ille vecors, hi autem impuberes es-sent, proceres atq; duces sibi imperium, veluti palmam, esse propositum existimarunt, & illud fore fortissimi atque fortunatissimi præ-mium.
units.tr: The cause of the division was that ambiguous saying of the dying Alexander, who, when asked whom he was leaving as successor, replied: "the most worthy." Hence, although he had a brother, two sons and a daughter, the nobles and commanders thought that the empire was set before them like a palm, and that it would be the prize of the bravest and most fortunate, since the brother was feeble-minded and the sons were not yet of age.

units.la: Quamdiu tamen aliquis ex Alexanxandri familia superfuit, abstinuerunt a titulo regio, eumq; concesserunt primo quidem Philippo Aridaeo, qui erat frater Alexandri, deinde filiis: Alexandro, Herculi, & tandem filiae Cleopatrae. Quibus omnibus necatis, tum demum in V. haec regna imperium Macedonicum diviserunt.
units.tr: As long as any member of Alexander's family survived, they refrained from taking the royal title, and first granted it to Philip Arrhidaeus, who was Alexander's brother, then to the sons Alexander and Hercules, and finally to the daughter Cleopatra. When all of these had been put to death, they at last divided the Macedonian empire into five kingdoms.

units.la: Ex regno Asiae nata regna Pergami, Bithyniae, Cappadociae, Ponti.
units.tr: From the kingdom of Asia arose the kingdoms of Pergamum, Bithynia, Cappadocia, Pontus.

units.la: Regnum Asiae invasit Antigonus, vetustissimus Ducum Alexandri, ludq; varia fortuna ad alium Demetrium transmisit, cum quo & extinctum fuit. Ex huius regni naufragio, veluti tabulae quaedam enatarunt regna Pergami, Bithyniae, Cappadociae & Ponti, quae paulo post in Romanorum potestatem concessere. Ca-
units.tr: Antigonus, the oldest of Alexander's commanders, seized the kingdom of Asia and, after varied fortune, passed it on to his son Demetrius, with whom it also came to an end. From the wreck of this kingdom, like certain planks, emerged the kingdoms of Pergamum, Bithynia, Cappadocia and Pontus, which shortly afterwards passed into the power of the Romans. Ca-

units.la: Canon 3. Thracia in Sapæos, Odrysas, & Galatas divisa est.
units.tr: Rule 3. Thrace was divided among the Sapaei, the Odrysae and the Galatians.

units.la: Regnum Thraciæ constituit Lysimachus: quo interfecto, terræ mo-tiones Thraciam divisere. Galatæ ex Galliâ in Græciam profecti in Thraciâ qvoqve regnum constituerunt, ut Polybius observavit. Ex qvo fabula illorum re-dargu'tur, qvi Galatas Duce Brenno in spoliatione templi Delphici ful-minibus & terræ motibus extinctos tradidere. Namid confictum suis-se à Græcis Polybius l. 4. v. 46. osten-dit, ac Galatas magno numero in Thraciam migrasse, ibiqve regnum celebre condidisse; cujusqve & Re-ges recenset.
units.tr: Lysimachus established the kingdom of Thrace; after his death, political upheavals divided Thrace. The Galatians, having set out from Gaul into Greece, also established a kingdom in Thrace, as Polybius observed. From this the fable is refuted of those who handed down that the Galatians, under their leader Brennus, were destroyed by lightning and earthquakes while plundering the temple at Delphi. For Polybius, bk. 4, ch. 46, shows that this story was invented by the Greeks, and that the Galatians migrated in large numbers into Thrace, where they founded a famous kingdom; and he also lists its kings.

units.la: Canon 4. Macedonia post varios momotus ad Alexandri familiam redit.
units.tr: Rule 4. Macedonia, after various upheavals, returned to the family of Alexander.

units.la: Macedonia enim fuerat diu præda occupantium, & miserè cùm ab externis hostibus, tùm civium discordiis distracta, donec Antigonus, Genatas[?], ex posteritate Alexandri, eam recuperaret. Ultimus Regum fuit Perseus à Romanis debellatus.
units.tr: Macedonia had for a long time been the prey of those who seized it, and was miserably torn both by foreign enemies and by civil discord, until Antigonus Gonatas, of the posterity of Alexander, recovered it. The last of its kings was Perseus, defeated by the Romans.

units.la: Syria defectione Parthorum, Bactrianorum, Indorum, Armeniorum, Medorum, Iudæorum, Arabum, debilitata fuit.
units.tr: Syria was weakened by the revolt of the Parthians, Bactrians, Indians, Armenians, Medes, Jews and Arabs.

units.la: Familiæ regum Syriæ Seleuci-dæ vocantur, a SeleucoNicanore, qui primus post Alexandrum Syriam & totum Orientem in suâ potestate habuit, usque quo ipsius posteri dome-sticis sticis[?] dissidiis se debilitarunt. Nam inde occasione arrepta Barbaræ nationes pleræq; defecerunt: ex quibus celeberrimi ac potentissimi postea fuerunt Parthi, qui soli Romana arma sustinuerunt, & victrices aquilas ad Euphratem subsistere jusserunt. Hoc Parthorum Imperium deinde translatum fuit ad Persas, quorum Reges communi nomine Chosrovv, i. e. latè regnantes dicebantur. Ultimus horum Regum fuit Jazdeshird, debellatus à Saracenis circa A. C. 650. Judæi quoq; ductu Maccabæorum à Syris defecerunt: quorum primus iterum post Zedechiam rex fuit Aristobulus: cui postea successit Herodes Magnus, sub quo excisum fuit regnum Judæorum à Vespasiano.
units.tr: The kings of Syria are called the Seleucids, from Seleucus Nicanor, who was the first after Alexander to hold Syria and the whole East in his power, until his descendants weakened themselves by domestic dissensions. For the barbarian nations, seizing the opportunity, mostly revolted from them; among these the Parthians later became most famous and most powerful, the only people who withstood Roman arms and ordered their victorious eagles to halt at the Euphrates. The empire of the Parthians was then transferred to the Persians, whose kings were commonly called Chosroes, that is, "widely reigning." The last of these kings was Yazdegerd, defeated by the Saracens around A.D. 650. The Jews also, under the leadership of the Maccabees, revolted from the Syrians; of these the first to be king again after Zedekiah was Aristobulus, who was succeeded by Herod the Great, under whom the kingdom of the Jews was destroyed by Vespasian.

units.la: Seleucida tot provinciis spoliati in exiguo Syriæ angulo regnârunt, donec Syri dedignati perpetuas ipsorum contentiones ad regnum evocarent Tigranem, Armeniorum regem: quo debellato, Cnejus Pompe-jus M. Syriam in Provinciae formam redegit.
units.tr: The Seleucids, stripped of so many provinces, reigned in a small corner of Syria, until the Syrians, weary of their constant quarrels, summoned Tigranes, king of the Armenians, to rule them; when he had been defeated, Gnaeus Pompey the Great reduced Syria to the form of a province.

units.la: Primus regum fuit Ptolemæus Lagi, cujus omnis posteritas Ptole-mæi dicta. Fuerunt autem omnes profligatissimæ vitæ, & monstra virorum. Ab Ægypto avulsum regnum Lybiæ aridæ, & Cyrenes, quod rex Ptolemæus Apion Romanis testamento legavit.
units.tr: The first of the kings was Ptolemy Lagus, and all his descendants were called Ptolemies. All of them, however, lived most abandoned lives and were monsters of men. The kingdom of arid Libya and Cyrene was torn away from Egypt; King Ptolemy Apion bequeathed it to the Romans by will.

units.la: Regum seriem clausit Cleopatra, uxor Marci Antonii, debellata ab Augusto. Sic totum Imperium Macedonicum ad Romanos concessit.
units.tr: Cleopatra, the wife of Mark Antony, who was defeated by Augustus, closed the series of kings. Thus the whole Macedonian empire passed to the Romans.
The Roman Empire was founded by Augustus.

units.la: Per quas mutationes & vicissitudines atque gradus respubl. Romana circumacta fuerit, donec veluti fessa & victoribus exhausta in finum Augusti se conjiceret, sefforemque[?] Augustum, veluti equus recalcitrando defatigatus, facile patere-tur, Tacit.l.1. Annal.c.1. compendio refert.
units.tr: By what changes, vicissitudes and stages the Roman commonwealth was driven about, until, as if weary and exhausted by its conquerors, it threw itself into the lap of Augustus, and Augustus, like a horse worn out by kicking back, easily let himself be mastered, Tacitus, Annals 1, ch. 1, relates in brief.

units.la: Sub Augusto igitur Imperium Romanorum demum obtinuit summum suum fastigium atq; perfectionem, sub quo etiam florentissimum fuit, ac pax per universum terrarum orbem; unde ipse Salvator Mundi Christus sub eô Imperatore nasci voluit.
units.tr: Under Augustus, therefore, the Roman Empire at last attained its highest summit and perfection; under him it also flourished most greatly, and there was peace throughout the whole orb of the earth. For this reason the Saviour of the World, Christ, willed to be born under that Emperor.
Constantine the Great divided the Empire.

units.la: Causa divisionis fuit translatæ sedes Imperii Romæ Constantino-polim.
units.tr: The cause of the division was the transfer of the seat of the Empire from Rome to Constantinople.

units.la: Primo Romanum Imperium divisum fuit in tres partes: Cisalpinam, Transalpinam, & Orientem: Deinde in Occidentem & Orientem. In Occidente Imperium mox defecit, ob barbaricas irruptiones; Ultimus Occidentalis Imperator fuit Romulus Momyllus Augustulus, in quo duo fatalia nomina concurrebant. Sicut enim Romulus urbem Romam fundaverat, Augustus Imperium; sic ultimus Romanus hic Imperator fatali quadam necessitate & Romuli & Augusti, sed minutum nomen habuit; & quod cunq; tùm Romulus, tùm Augustus construxerant, sub ipso Barbari di-ruerunt.
units.tr: First, the Roman Empire was divided into three parts: Cisalpine, Transalpine and Eastern; then into West and East. In the West the Empire soon failed, owing to barbarian invasions. The last Western emperor was Romulus Momyllus Augustulus, in whom two fateful names came together. For as Romulus had founded the city of Rome and Augustus the Empire, so this last Roman emperor, by a certain fated necessity, bore the names of both Romulus and Augustus, though a diminished name. And whatever Romulus and Augustus had built up, the barbarians tore down under him.

units.la: Orientis Imperium permul-ta adhuc secula floruit: Sed & il-lud partim à Scythis, partim à Saracenis ita debilitatum fuit, ut præter urbem Constantinopolim & vicinas quasdam provincias vix quicquam obtineret, donec tandem A.C.1453. h. e. ante 200. ferè annosà Mahummede Turcarum Imperatore, captâ Constantinopoli penitùs extinguere,[?] tur;
units.tr: The Eastern Empire flourished for many centuries more. But it too was so weakened, partly by the Scythians and partly by the Saracens, that apart from the city of Constantinople and some neighbouring provinces it hardly held anything; until at last, in the year 1453, that is about 200 years ago, when Mahomet was Emperor of the Turks and Constantinople had been taken, it was finally extinguished.

units.la: Historia recentior est vel Orientalis, vel Occidentalis vel Australis.
units.tr: Recent history is either Eastern, or Western, or Southern.

units.la: Orientalis est vel Scythi-ca, vel Æthiopica vel Sinensis.
units.tr: Eastern history is either Scythian, or Ethiopian, or Chinese.

units.la: Scythica est vel Germani-ca, vel Hunnica, vel Slavoni-ca.
units.tr: Scythian history is either Germanic, or Hunnic, or Slavonic.

units.la: Germanica est vel Gothica, vel Francica, vel Anglo-Saxo-nica.
units.tr: Germanic history is either Gothic, or Frankish, or Anglo-Saxon.

units.la: Gothica est vel Normanni-ca, vel Ost-Gothica, vel West-Gothica.
units.tr: Gothic history is either Norman, or East-Gothic, or West-Gothic.

units.la: Normannica est vel Scandzica, vel Sicula.
units.tr: Norman history is either Scandzian, or Sicilian.
Scandzica comprises the affairs of Denmark, Sweden and Norway.

units.la: Omnes illæ regiones, quæ tria regna Septentrionalia complectuntur, uno nomine ab antiquis rerum Gothicarum Scriptoribus vocantur Scandia & Scandinavia,
units.tr: All those regions that make up the three northern kingdoms are called by one name, Scandia and Scandinavia, by the ancient writers on Gothic affairs.

units.la: Dania, Norvvegia & Svecia freqventer conjuncta & disjuncta regna fuerunt.
units.tr: Denmark, Norway and Sweden were kingdoms that were often joined and often separate.

units.la: Antiqvissima horum regnorum menmentio extat apud Tacitum (Germ. 45, ii.) sub Svionum nomine, per quos intelligit Svecos, & Sitonum, qui videntur esse Norvvegi.
units.tr: The earliest mention of these kingdoms is found in Tacitus (Germ. 45), under the name of the Sviones, by whom he means the Swedes, and the Sitones, who seem to be the Norwegians.

units.la: Norvvegia olim quam plu-res habuit Reges, donec ad u-nius potestatem perveniret.
units.tr: Norway once had several kings, until it came under the power of one alone.

units.la: Temporibus Caroli M. vocabatur Normannia, ejus incolæ Normanni, piratica & excursionibus suis[?] in universam illis seculis Europam famosi: Unde in templis Christianorum hæc solennis precandi formula tunc recepta fuit: A furore Normannorum libera nos Domine.
units.tr: In the time of Charlemagne it was called Normannia, and its inhabitants Normans, notorious in those centuries for piracy and their raids across the whole of Europe. Hence the following solemn form of prayer was then adopted in the churches of the Christians: From the fury of the Normans, deliver us, O Lord.

units.la: Primus universæ Norvvegiæ Rex & Monarcha factus fuit Haraldus Harfagerus sive Pulchricomus, conditor regiæ Harfagerorum familiæ, qvæ ab A. C. 878. usqve ad annum 1388. continuâ successione regnavit.
units.tr: The first to become king and sole ruler of all Norway was Harald Harfager, that is, Fair-hair, founder of the royal family of the Harfagers, which reigned in unbroken succession from 878 A.D. until 1388.
Canon 3. Iceland and Greenland are colonies of the Norwegians.

units.la: Qvam prisci appellarunt Thu. lem, ultimam omnium Infularum, ea à Norvvegis Islandia dicta fuit. Cùm enim Haraldus Harfagerus reliquos reguios totâ Norvvegiâ pelleret, multi tyrannidé ipsius fugientes circa A. C. 900 in Islandiam adhuc incultam navigarunt, eamq; habitare cæperunt. Cumq; initio liberi ac sui juris essent, tandem reges Norvvegiæ ipsos potestati suæ subjecerunt.
units.tr: The island that the ancients called Thule, the furthest of all the islands, was called Iceland by the Norwegians. For when Harald Harfager drove the remaining petty kings out of all Norway, many who fled his tyranny sailed around 900 A.D. to the still uninhabited Iceland, and began to live there. And although at first they were free and under their own law, the kings of Norway eventually brought them under their power.

units.la: Ex Islandia qvidam Ericus Ruf-sus coloniam duxit in ultimam terrarum Gronlandiam. Hujus Gronlandiæ terrarum pariter ac hominum omnis notitia periit circa A. C.1416. neque hactenus reperiri potuit: nam quæ hodie Gronlandia appellatur, hominibus destituta & alia regio est. Causam referunt tum in pestilentiam quandam, tum in glaciem ex mari Tartarico tempestatibus eje-ctam, quæ omnes in Gronlandia additus obstruxit. Unde quidam Gronlandos vel pestilentiâ extinctos putant, vel litoribus desertis ad inte-riora & remotiora, ac ut Hugo Grotius voluit, in ipsam Americam septentrionalem migrasse putant.
units.tr: From Iceland a certain Eric the Red led a colony to the furthest land, Greenland. All knowledge of this land of Greenland, and of its people, was lost around 1416 A.D. and has not been found to this day; for what is today called Greenland is another region, destitute of people. They give as the cause either a certain plague, or ice driven from the Tartar Sea by storms, which blocked all the approaches to Greenland. Hence some think the Greenlanders either died out from the plague, or, having deserted the coasts, moved into the interior and more remote parts; and, as Hugo Grotius preferred, that they migrated into North America itself.
The Normans founded the kingdoms of both Sicilies.

units.la: Quod nunc in Italia Neapolitanum vocatur regnum, olim Sicilia cis Farum sive Fretum; insula vero, Sicilia trans Farum dicebatur.
units.tr: What is now called in Italy the kingdom of Naples was formerly Sicily this side of the Pharos, or strait; the island itself was called Sicily beyond the Pharos.

units.la: Ab his ad Svevos, Andegavenses & Aragonios pervenit.
units.tr: From them it passed to the Swabians, the Angevins and the Aragonese.

units.la: Tancredus cum manu Normannorum in Apulia, captis aliquot oppidis, consedit. Ejus Filius Drago A.C. 1039. primus Apuliæ Comes creatus fuit. Wilhelmus Ferrobrachium Calabriam & Capuam; Robertus Guiscardus, à Bettimeo Saracenorum Principe Catanensi, in Siciliam evocatus, Messanam, Panormum, & magnam Siciliæ partem occupavit, eamque; fratri suo Rogerio Bof-fo[?] reliquit, qui primus Siciliæ Comes dictus fuit.
units.tr: Tancred, with a band of Normans, settled in Apulia, after capturing several towns. His son Drogo was the first made Count of Apulia, in 1039 A.D. William Ironarm took Calabria and Capua; Robert Guiscard, summoned to Sicily by Bettimus, prince of the Saracens of Catania, occupied Messina, Palermo and a large part of Sicily, and left it to his brother Roger Boffo, who was the first to be called Count of Sicily.

units.la: Extincta Roberti Guiscardi progenie Rogerius II, Comes Siciliæ Apuliam, Calabriam, Capuam, ditiones fraternas, Siciliæ conjunxit, ac priprimus titulum Siciliæ ac Italiæ Re-gis usurpavit,
units.tr: When the line of Robert Guiscard had died out, Roger II, Count of Sicily, joined to Sicily the Apulian, Calabrian and Capuan domains of his brothers, and was the first to assume the title of King of Sicily and Italy.

units.la: Tum captô Innocentio II. & ho-norificè dimissô Rogerius ab eo Ne-apoli & aliis Græcorum regionibus donatus est; ejus tamen svasu titu-lô Regis Italiæ abstinuit; contentus Regem Siciliæ, Ducem Apuliæ & Calabriæ, Principem Capuæ, Neapolis, Salerni, Amalfis Dominum se appel-lare. Heinricus IV. Imperator Ro-gerio III. Siciliam & Neapolin ade-mit relictis ei tantùm Ducatu Taren-tino & Comitatu Lucaniæ, qvæ tamen paulò post etiam Ducatui Svevia ad-jecit. Ultimus ex familia Ducum Svevia Rex Siciliæ & Neapolis fuit Conradinus, quem Carolus Andega-vensis decollari jussit.
units.tr: Then, having captured Innocent II and dismissed him with honour, Roger was granted Naples and other regions of the Greeks by him; yet at his urging he refrained from the title of King of Italy, being content to call himself King of Sicily, Duke of Apulia and Calabria, Prince of Capua, and Lord of Naples, Salerno and Amalfi. Emperor Henry IV stripped Roger III of Sicily and Naples, leaving him only the Duchy of Taranto and the County of Lucania, which, however, shortly afterwards he also added to the Duchy of Swabia. The last of the family of the Dukes of Swabia to be King of Sicily and Naples was Conradin, whom Charles of Anjou ordered to be beheaded.

units.la: Ita regnum Siciliæ & Neapolis ad familiam Andegavensem pervenit. A C.1270. Amissâ per vesperas Si-culas A. C. 1282, Siciliâ Carolus Re-
units.tr: Thus the kingdom of Sicily and Naples passed to the Angevin family. In 1270 A.D., after Sicily was lost through the Sicilian Vespers in 1282 A.D., Charles,

units.la: Regem Neapolis fe appellavit Ex hac familia duæ flagitiosæ Johannæ regnarunt, post qvas Alphonfus Sapiens Rex Aragonia Neapolim obti-nuit
units.tr: called himself King of Naples. Two wicked queens named Joanna reigned from this family, after whom Alphonso the Wise, King of Aragon, obtained Naples.

units.la: Occasio fuit obitus Alphonsi Sapientis sine prole legitima. Cùm enim ei testamento successisset Fer-dinandi filius illegitimus, Carolus IIX[?] Rex Galliæ, juvenis gloriæ & imperii avidus, regnum Neapolitanum felicissimo bello expugnavit. Sed Gallos mox iterum hac prædâ spoliarunt Hispani: Cùm enim Ludovi-cus XII. Rex Galliæ, & Ferdinandus Rex Hispaniæ, initiò regnum Neapolitanum partiti fuissent, mox ortis de finibus controversiis Galli
units.tr: The occasion was the death of Alphonso the Wise without legitimate offspring. For when an illegitimate son of Ferdinand had succeeded him by will, Charles VIII [?], King of France, a young man greedy for glory and empire, conquered the kingdom of Naples in a most fortunate war. But the Spaniards soon despoiled the French of this prey again: for when Louis XII, King of France, and Ferdinand, King of Spain, had at first divided the kingdom of Naples between them, controversies over the boundaries soon arose, and the French were

units.la: B toto regno pulsi sunt, A. C. 1504.
units.tr: driven from the whole kingdom, in the year of Christ 1504.
The Neapolitans unsuccessfully aspired to liberty several times.

units.la: Primò quidem A. C. 1570. deinde 1647. Duce quodam piscatore, cui nomen Thomas Aniello sive contractè Mas Aniello. Cujus historia ut in recenti adhuc memoria, ita plena miraculorum.
units.tr: First indeed in the year of Christ 1570, then in 1647, under a certain fisherman named Thomas Aniello, or in contracted form Masaniello. His history, as it is still in recent memory, is so full of miracles.
The Ostrogoths obtained the kingdom of Italy.

units.la: Cum Romanorum Imperium in Romulo Momyllo Augustulo extinctū fuisset, Theodoricus Ostgotho-rum Rex, superato Odoacro Rege He-rurulorum [?] & Rhugiorum, Italiæ Rex factus fuit A. C. 493. Ultimus Ost-Gothorum Rex in Italia fuit Totilas, quem Narses Justiniani I. Imperatoris Dux vitâ ac regnô exuit. Sed paulô post Longobardi, ductu regis sui Alboini, eandem Italiam Roma-nis eripuerunt: à quibus hodieque Italiæ pars Longobardia dicitur. Hi Longobardi regnarunt usq; ad Ca-rolum M. qui Italiam recuperavit.
units.tr: When the Roman Empire was extinguished in Romulus Augustulus, Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths, defeated Odoacer, king of the Heruli [?] and Rugians, and became king of Italy in AD 493. The last king of the Ostrogoths in Italy was Totila, whom Narses, the general of the emperor Justinian I, stripped of life and kingdom. But shortly afterwards the Lombards, under their king Alboin, snatched the same Italy from the Romans; from them that part of Italy is still called Lombardy today. These Lombards reigned until Charlemagne, who recovered Italy.

units.la: Westgothi Rege Athaulfo sive Adolpho expugnatâ Româ in Galliam, & inde sub Rege Theodorico in Hispaniam migrarunt, eamq; totam
units.tr: Under King Athaulf, also called Adolphus, after the capture of Rome, the West Goths migrated into Gaul, and from there under King Theodoric into Spain, and they subjected the whole of it to their rule.

units.la: Imperio suo subjecerunt: Unde hodieq; tota Hispaniae Nobilitas originem suam deducit à Westgothis.
units.tr: Hence even today the entire Spanish nobility traces its origin to the Westgoths.

units.la: Hoc regnum Westgothicum in Hispania destructum fuit à Mauris.
units.tr: This West Gothic kingdom in Spain was destroyed by the Moors.

units.la: A. C, 713. sub ultimo Rege Gothorum Roderico. Causa fuit hujus calamitatis, quod Rodericus Cavam, Juliani Comitis Mauritaniae filiam, stuprasset. Quapropter Julianus, ut sumeret ultionem de Roderico, Saracenos ex Mauritania ad Hispaniam occupandam evocavit, qui vi-ctoRoderico universa breviter tempore potiti sunt Hispaniā.
units.tr: This happened in AD 713, under the last Gothic king, Roderick. The cause of this calamity was that Roderick had violated Cava, the daughter of Julian, count of Mauretania. Therefore Julian, to take revenge on Roderick, summoned the Saracens from Mauretania to occupy Spain, and they, having defeated Roderick, soon took possession of the whole of Spain.

units.la: Gothi quinque regna per Hispaniam pulsis Mauris instaurarunt. Ex-
units.tr: The Goths restored five kingdoms across Spain after the Moors were driven out. Ex-

units.la: Quicunq; hanc calamitatem eva-serant Gothi in altissimos ac inaccef-sos montes Asturiæ, Cantabriæ & Pyrenæorum se receperunt, & inde excursionibus in plana ac circumja-centia factis, aliquot oppida à Mau-ris recuperarunt, novosq; sibi Reges præfecerunt.
units.tr: When the Goths had escaped this calamity, they withdrew to the highest and inaccessible mountains of Asturia, Cantabria and the Pyrenees. From there, by making raids into the plains and surrounding regions, they recovered several towns from the Moors and set up new kings for themselves.
The first kingdom was established in Asturia.

units.la: A. C. 716. Primus Rex fuit Pelagius ex veterum Regum Gothorum sanguine. Sedes Regia fuit initio urbs Ovetum, deinde Legio. Unde hodieqve regnum Legionis inter titulos Regis Hispaniæ primum locum obtinet.
units.tr: In A.D. 716 the first king was Pelagius, of the blood of the old Gothic kings. The royal seat was at first the city of Ovetum, then Legio. Hence even today the kingdom of León holds the first place among the titles of the King of Spain.
The second kingdom was founded in the Pyrenean mountains.

units.la: Circa A. C. 724. Hoc regnum di-cebatur initio Soprarba & Ripagorza: deinde capta Pampejopoli sive Pampelonâ dictum fuit regnum Pampelona; & tandem, quod nomen hodieq; obtinet, Navarra.
units.tr: Around A.D. 724. This kingdom was at first called Soprarba and Ripagorza. Then, after Pampejopolis or Pampelona was taken, the kingdom was called Pampelona. Finally, under the name it still bears today, it is Navarra.

units.la: Aragonia primò fuit comita-tus; deinde A. C. 895. Sanctius Ka-so Arbaca regem sese Aragoniæ appellavit.
units.tr: Aragon was at first a county. Then, in A.D. 895, Sanctius Kaso Arbaca styled himself king of Aragon.

units.la: Cæpit A. C. 1139. Primus Rex fuit Alphonsus.
units.tr: It began in A.D. 1139. The first king was Alphonsus.

units.la: Hæc initiô Comitatus fuit: Primô Ferdinandus M. A. C. 1035. Castiliæ regem se appellavit.
units.tr: This was at first a county. In A.D. 1035 Ferdinand the Great first called himself king of Castilia.
The Moors were at last driven out of all Spain.

units.la: A C 1492[?] capta urbe Grana-da Maurorum Imperio per Hispaniam finis impositus fuit, cum ei per 700. annos incubassent.
units.tr: In A.D. 1492[?], with the city of Granada taken, the rule of the Moors over Spain was brought to an end, after they had lain upon it for 700 years.

units.la: Reges Castiliæ & Portugalliæ Indiam Orientalem & occidentalem aperuerunt.
units.tr: The kings of Castile and Portugal opened up the East and West Indies.

units.la: Eodem anno, quo Granada Mauris erepta Christophorus Columbus, auauspiciis Ferdinandi Catholici Regis Aragoniae & Castiliae novum & hactenus plane incognitum orbem, quem Americam vocamus, detexit. Paulò post Portugalli duce Vasco de Gama Africam circumvecti in Orientalem Indiam penetrarunt. A quo tempore Hispania opibus & potentiâ immane quantum crevit.
units.tr: In the same year in which Granada was snatched from the Moors, Christopher Columbus, under the auspices of Ferdinand the Catholic, king of Aragon and Castile, discovered the new and hitherto wholly unknown world which we call America. Shortly afterwards, the Portuguese under their leader Vasco de Gama sailed round Africa and penetrated into the East Indies. From that time Spain grew immensely in wealth and power.
Philip II gained possession of all Spain.

units.la: A.C.1580. Ita regnum Hispaniae potentiâ summum veluti suum fastigium obtinuit, & sparsum per omnes Orbis partes imperium exercuit.
units.tr: In A.D. 1580 the kingdom of Spain thus reached the summit of its power, as it were its peak, and exercised dominion spread across every part of the world.

units.la: Primo qviden[?] defectione Pro-vinciarum Belgicarum, quæ facta A. C. 1581. deinde defectione Portugal-liæ A. C. 1640. Belgæ enim Rem-publicam instituerunt & Portugalli Regem Johannem Bragantiæ Du-cem crearunt.
units.tr: First, indeed, by the revolt of the Belgian Provinces, which took place in A.D. 1581; then by the revolt of Portugal in A.D. 1640. For the Belgians set up a commonwealth, and the Portuguese made John, Duke of Braganza, their king.

units.la: Prima mentio Francorum in tempora Imperatoris Probi incidit.
units.tr: The first mention of the Franks falls in the time of the Emperor Probus.

units.la: Nam qvicunqve populi per Germaniam & Galliam à Romanis deficiebant Franci,i. e. Liberi homines dicebantur.
units.tr: For whatever peoples across Germany and Gaul revolted from the Romans were called Franks, that is, free men.
The first King of the Franks was Marcomer.

units.la: Electus[?] A. C. 418. Ei postan-num successit Faramundus, a quo vulgo series Regum Franciae deducitur. Huic successit Clodio Comatus. Et hi in Germania regnarunt. Primus autem Merovingus Galliam occupavit, quae in posterum Francia dicta fuit. Ab hoc Merovingo primo Regum Franciae familia vocatur Merovingorum, sub quibus regnum Franciae aliquoties divisum fuit in haec quatuor regna: 1. in regnum Franciae sive Parisiorum. 2. in regnum Belgicae, cujus sedes urbs Suessionum. 3. in regnum Aurelianorum, cujus sedes Aurelianum. 4. in regnum Austrasiae, cujus sedes urbs Mediomatricum sive Metz.
units.tr: He was elected in the year 418 after Christ. He was succeeded by Pharamond, from whom the series of the Kings of France is commonly traced. He was succeeded by Clodio Comatus. These ruled in Germany. But Merovech was the first to occupy Gaul, which afterwards was called France. From this Merovech the first royal family of the Franks is called the Merovingians, under whom the kingdom of the Franks was divided several times into these four kingdoms: (1) the kingdom of the Franks, or of the Parisians; (2) the kingdom of Belgica, whose seat was the city of Soissons; (3) the kingdom of the Aurelians, whose seat was Orléans; (4) the kingdom of Austrasia, whose seat was the city of Mediomatricum, or Metz.
The Carolingians stripped the Merovingians of the kingdom.

units.la: Causa fuit socordia Merovingo-rum, qui, veluti Sardanapali, omnem regni curam in Majores Domus re-jiciebant, à quibus tandem regno plane spoliati sunt, tanquam indigni. Memorabile est, hos Merovingos se-mel tantum in anno, nimirum die Paschatis, corollâ florea redimitos populo conspiciendas se præbuisse in plaustro rustico, quod ad majo-rem contemtum boves trahebant.
units.tr: The cause was the indolence of the Merovingians, who, like Sardanapalus, left all the care of the kingdom to the Mayors of the Palace. In the end they were stripped of the kingdom altogether, as unworthy of it. It is worth noting that these Merovingians showed themselves to the people only once a year, namely on Easter Day, crowned with a garland of flowers and riding in a rustic wagon, which oxen drew, to make them an even greater object of contempt.

units.la: Pipinus igitur, cognomine Par-vus, consensu Zachariæ Pontificis Romani Chilpericum stupidum, ultimum ex familia Merovingorum, in Monasterium detrusit, & se Regem Franciæ constituit. Ejus filius fuit Carolus Magnus.
units.tr: Accordingly, Pepin, surnamed the Short, with the consent of Zachary, the Roman Pontiff, thrust Childeric the Dullard, the last of the Merovingian family, into a monastery, and made himself King of the Franks. His son was Charlemagne.

units.la: Sub Carolo M. regnum Francorum florentissimum fuit.
units.tr: Under Charlemagne the kingdom of the Franks flourished most of all.

units.la: Ab hoc secunda familia Regnum Franciæ vocatur Carolingorum. Hic Carolus devictâ Germaniâ & Longobardiâ sive Italiâ, extinctam Romani Imperii in Occidente inde usq; à Romulo Momyllo Augustulo majestatem A. C. 800. iterum restituit, & Imperator Romanorum à Leone III. Pontifice Romano coronatus fuit, acclamante populo Romano: Carolo Augusto à Deo coronato Pio, Felici, vita, salus & victoria.
units.tr: From him the second family is called the Carolingian dynasty. This Charles, having conquered Germany and Lombardy or Italy, restored in the year 800 the majesty of the Roman Empire in the West, which had been extinct since Romulus Augustulus, and he was crowned Emperor of the Romans by Leo III, the Roman Pontiff, while the Roman people acclaimed: To Charles Augustus, crowned by God, pious and fortunate, life, safety and victory.

units.la: Plerique per Galliam, Belgium & Germaniam Principatus à Carolingis instituti.
units.tr: Most of the principalities in Gaul, Belgium and Germany were founded by the Carolingians.

units.la: Nam Carolus M. Ducatum Sa-xonia xoniæ, Westphaliæ & Angliæ instituit; ex quibus Comitatus Oldenbur-gensis & alii plurimi orti sunt.
units.tr: For Charlemagne established the duchies of Saxony, Westphalia and England; from these arose the county of Oldenburg and very many others.

units.la: Deficiente Carolingorum & virtute & familiâ, Germani Conra-dum Franconiæ Ducem Imperato-rem crearunt: Et ab eo tempore nullum Franciæ Regem ad Imperi-um admittere voluerunt.
units.tr: With the Carolingians failing both in strength and in family, the Germans created Conrad, Duke of Franconia, as Emperor; and from that time they were unwilling to admit any King of France to the empire.
The kingdom of France comes to the Capetians.

units.la: Tertia familia Regum Franciæ est Capetingorum, ita dicta ab Hugone Capeto Comite Parisiorum, qui exclusis Carolingis regnum Franciæ invasit: eaq; familia hodieque regnat.
units.tr: The third family of the Kings of France is that of the Capetians, so called from Hugh Capet, Count of Paris, who, with the Carolingians excluded, seized the kingdom of France; and this family reigns to this day.
Canon 3. The Capetians are divided into Valois and Bourbons.

units.la: Extinctâ rectâ Capetingorum lineâ regnum Galliæ pervenit ad Philippum Comitem Valesiorum A. C. 1328. Sed huic Successioni acerrimè sese oppoluit Eduardus III, Rex Angliæ. Inde diuturna illa & hor-renda bella inter Anglos & Francos orta fuerunt. Nam Eduardus erat proprior Sanguine; Philippus jure: illum excludebat Lex Salica; hunc admittebat.
units.tr: With the direct line of the Capetians extinct, the kingdom of France passed in the year 1328 to Philip, Count of Valois. But Edward III, King of England, opposed this succession most fiercely. Hence arose those long and dreadful wars between the English and the French. For Edward was nearer by blood, Philip by right: the Salic Law excluded the former and admitted the latter.

units.la: Sub hoc Philippo Valesio Delphinatus Franciæ regno accessit, mortuo Delphino, unico ejus hæredi: cujus jacturam pater Humbertus adeò immoderatè tulit, ut Ducatum Philippo Valesio eâ conditione donaret, ut primogenitus Regis Franciæ appellaretur Delphinus.
units.tr: Under this Philip of Valois, the Dauphiné was added to the kingdom of France, on the death of the Dauphin, its only heir; his father Humbert bore the loss so immoderately that he gave the duchy to Philip of Valois on the condition that the eldest son of the King of France should be called the Dauphin.

units.la: Familia Valesiorum extincta fuit in Henrico III. A. C. 1589. Regnum igitur jure Legis Salicæ translatum fuit ad stirpem Borbonicam, cujus tunc caput erat Henricus Rex Navarræ, dictus postea IV. sive Magnus. Ei successit Ludovicus XIII. & qui nunc rebus Galliæ præest Ludovicus XIV.
units.tr: The family of the Valois became extinct in Henry III in the year 1589. The kingdom therefore passed by right of the Salic Law to the Bourbon stock, whose head was then Henry, King of Navarre, afterwards called Henry IV or the Great. He was succeeded by Louis XIII, and the one who now presides over the affairs of France is Louis XIV.

units.la: Imperium Germaniæ à Francis ad Saxones; alternatim ab his ad Svevos; deinde ad diversas familias; denique ad Austriacos devenit.
units.tr: The empire of Germany passed from the Franks to the Saxons; alternately from these to the Swabians; then to various families; and at last came to the Austrians.

units.la: Cùm Germania à Francorum regno secessionem fecisset, Imperatores sibi liberis suffragiis ex suâ ratione præfecerunt: plerunq; autem ex potentissimis familiis Saxonum, Francorum, Svevorum, Bavarorum & tandem Austriacorum.
units.tr: When Germany had seceded from the kingdom of the Franks, the emperors were set over themselves by free votes, according to their own judgement; yet for the most part from the most powerful families of the Saxons, Franks, Swabians, Bavarians, and at last of the Austrians.
Under Henry the Fowler the marches were established.

units.la: Causa fuit Hungarorum, Polono-rum[?], Slavorum, Vandalorum, Danorum ac Normannorum in Germaniam frequentes irruptiones. Heinricus igitur Auceps A. C. 927. contra Henetos[?] constituit Marchionatum Brandeburgensem, nec non contra Danos Slesvicensem; A. C. 928. contra Hungaros Austriacum; A. C. 930 contra Bohemos, Polonos, Silesios, Misnicum.
units.tr: The cause was the frequent incursions into Germany of the Hungarians, Poles[?], Slavs, Vandals, Danes and Normans. Henry the Fowler therefore, in the year 927, established the Brandenburg march against the Henetians[?], and likewise the Schleswig march against the Danes; in 928 the Austrian march against the Hungarians; in 930 the Meissen march against the Bohemians, Poles and Silesians.

units.la: Sub Ottone I. maxima Imperii Germanici potentia fuit.
units.tr: Under Otto I the power of the German Empire was at its greatest.

units.la: Otto I. à rebus gestis Magnus appellatus collapsam Imperii post Carolum M. dignitatem restituit. Sub ipsius nepote Ottone III. instituti Electores putantur; quanquam nihil certi eâ de re constet.
units.tr: Otto I, called the Great from his deeds, restored the dignity of the empire, which had collapsed after Charlemagne. Under his nephew Otto III the electors are thought to have been instituted, although nothing certain is known about this matter.

units.la: Miserrima Germaniæ con-ditio fuit post mortem Friderici II. durante interregno.
units.tr: The condition of Germany was most wretched after the death of Frederick II, during the interregnum.

units.la: Extinctâ Friderici II. familiâ, Germania XXII. continuos annos Imperatore caruit. Unde mira pas-sim confusio, latrocinia vaga, & quicquid malorum remotô à Republ. capite oriri solet.
units.tr: With the family of Frederick II extinct, Germany was without an emperor for twenty-two successive years. Hence everywhere great confusion, roving brigandage, and whatever evils usually arise when the head of the commonwealth is removed.

units.la: Eô tempore tota Germania arcibus & castellis impleta fuit, ex quibus se invicem deprædabantur, & quorum rudera hodieqve in montibus conspiciuntur.
units.tr: At that time the whole of Germany was filled with fortresses and castles, from which they plundered one another, and whose ruins are still seen on the mountains today.

units.la: Tandem electus fuit Imperator Rudolphus Comes Habsburgensis, a quo hodierna familia Austriaca originem ducit.
units.tr: At last Rudolph, Count of Habsburg, was elected emperor, and from him the present Austrian family takes its origin.

units.la: Carolus IV cum in Imperio ordinem constituit, qui ho-dieq; obtinet.
units.tr: Charles IV established the order in the empire which still prevails today.

units.la: A.C. 1353. publicata Aurea Bulla, quæ est Lex Imperii Romano-Germanici perpetua. Sed idem Carolus IV. vehementer debilitavit Impe-rium telonibus & reditibus Electo-ribus oppignoratis, ut filium suum Wenceslaum Imperatorem crea-rent.
units.tr: In 1353 the Golden Bull was published, which is the perpetual law of the Roman-German Empire. But the same Charles IV greatly weakened the empire by pledging the tolls and revenues to the electors, so that they would make his son Wenceslaus emperor.
Charles V was the most powerful of all the emperors.

units.la: Quippe qui cum Imperio amplissima Hispaniæ regna & ditiones Austriacas conjunxit,
units.tr: Indeed, he joined to the empire the very extensive kingdoms of Spain and the Austrian dominions,

units.la: Pax Monasterienfis Imperii statum vehementer mutavit.
units.tr: The Peace of Münster greatly changed the state of the empire.

units.la: Quippe inter cætera contra Au-ream Bullam octavus Electoratus constitutus fuit, titulo Archi Thesaurarii: Galliæ quoq; & Sveciæ Reges, ille Alsatiam, hic Pomeraniam, Episcopatum Bremensem & Verdensem adepti sunt.
units.tr: Indeed, among other things, contrary to the Golden Bull an eighth electorate was established, with the title of Arch-Treasurer; and the Kings of France and of Sweden also obtained, the one Alsace, the other Pomerania, and the bishoprics of Bremen and Verden.

units.la: Anglo-Saxones in Britannia septem Regna constituerunt.
units.tr: The Anglo-Saxons established seven kingdoms in Britain.

units.la: Causa fuit qvotidiana Scotorum & Pictorum in Britanniam irruptio. Unde Britanni, cùm frustrà à Romanis auxilia petiissent, Saxones è Germania evocarûnt, qui permixti Anglis & Frisiis magnô numerô transfretarunt, & pulsis Scotis, allecti Insulæ pulcritudine, ipsos Britannos ejecerunt, septemq; regna constituerunt.
units.tr: The cause was the daily incursion of the Scots and Picts into Britain. Hence the Britons, having sought help from the Romans in vain, summoned the Saxons from Germany. Mingled with the Angles and Frisians, they crossed the sea in great numbers, and, having driven out the Scots and being drawn by the beauty of the island, they expelled the Britons themselves and founded seven kingdoms.

units.la: Primum regnum fuit Cantii, fundatum A. C. 449. ab Hengisto.
units.tr: The first kingdom was that of Kent, founded in AD 449 by Hengist.

units.la: Secundum Suthsexia, fundatum A. C. 488 ab Ella: Tertium West-Saxonum, fundatum A.C. 519 à Cerdicio : Quartum East-Saxonum, fundatum A. C. 547. ab Ida: Quintum Nordanhumbria: Sextum East-Anglorum, fundatum A.C. 574. ab Uffa: Septimum Merciorum, fundatum A. C. 656. à Penda.
units.tr: The second was Sussex, founded in AD 488 by Ælle; the third, that of the West Saxons, founded in AD 519 by Cerdic; the fourth, that of the East Saxons, founded in AD 547 by Ida; the fifth was Northumbria; the sixth, that of the East Angles, founded in AD 574 by Uffa; the seventh, that of the Mercians, founded in AD 656 by Penda.

units.la: Canon 2. Inter hos septem Reges Anglo-Saxonum semper penes unum aliquem Monarchia fuit.
units.tr: Canon 2. Among these seven kings of the Anglo-Saxons, the monarchy always lay with one or another of them.

units.la: Id quod testatur Beda l. 7. Illa vero Monarchia fuit ambulatoria, modò penes hanc, modò penes aliam gentem, non successione vel electione, sed armis ac potentia quaerenda.
units.tr: This is attested by Bede, book 7. That monarchy, however, was itinerant, now resting with this people, now with that one, and it was to be sought not by succession or election but by arms and power.

units.la: Can. I. Septem regna Anglo-Saxonum in unum Angliæ Impe-rium coaluerunt.
units.tr: Canon 1. The seven kingdoms of the Anglo-Saxons coalesced into one empire of England.

units.la: A.C. 800. Rex West-Saxonum Ebertus primus factus fuit perpetuus Monarcha septem Regnorum: Ac abrogato Saxonum nomine universam gentem appellare voluit Anglos, & regnum Angliæ.
units.tr: In AD 800 the king of the West Saxons, Egbert, first became perpetual monarch of the seven kingdoms. Abolishing the name Saxons, he wished the whole nation to be called Angles, and the kingdom England.
After the Anglo-Saxons, the Danes gained the kingdom.

units.la: A.C. 1013[?]. Sveno Rex Danorum Angliam expugnavit. Ei successit filius Canutus M.alio nomine dictus Lamprecht. Permansit Anglia in potestate Danorum 26 annos usque ad 1042, quo omnes per Angliam Dani, conspiratione incolarum, unā die trucidati fuere, & regnum restitutum Eduardo Confessori legitimo regni hæredi.
units.tr: AD 1013[?]. Sweyn, king of the Danes, conquered England. He was succeeded by his son Canute the Great, also called Lamprecht by another name. England remained under Danish power for 26 years, until 1042, when all the Danes throughout England were slaughtered on a single day by a conspiracy of the inhabitants, and the kingdom was restored to Edward the Confessor, the lawful heir of the realm.

units.la: A.C. 1066. Wilhelmus Normanniæ Dux Angliam cruentâ victoriâ subjugavit, & dictus propterea Conquestor. Hæc Normannica invasio & lingvam, & mores & leges Anglorum vehementer mutavit.
units.tr: AD 1066. William, Duke of Normandy, subdued England by a bloody victory and was therefore called the Conqueror. This Norman invasion greatly altered the language, customs and laws of the English.

units.la: A.C. 117ʒ[?] Rege Heinrico II. Causa fuit raptus, quem Dermitius Rex Lagenia commiserat. Hâc oc-casione evocati in Hyberniam Angli universam Insulam debellarunt.
units.tr: AD 117[?], in the reign of Henry II. The cause was an abduction which Dermot, king of Leinster, had committed. On this occasion the English, called into Ireland, subdued the whole island.
The factions of the Lancastrians and the Yorkists grievously afflicted England.

units.la: Hæ factiones ab Historicis alio nomine vocantur Rosa rubra & Rosa alba. Nam Eboracenses se albam Ro-sam vocarunt, Lancastrenses se ru-bram nuncuparunt. Quantum mali ab hisce factionibus in Angliam dimanaverit ex Philippo Commineo inprimis videre est. Extinctæ fue-runt ab Henrico VII. qui ducta Eli-sabetha Regis Eduardi IV. silia Ro-sam albam, i. e. domum Eboracensem cum Rosa rubrâ e. Lancastren-si conjunxit. Unde hodieq; inter insignia Regum Angliæ duplex rosa conspicitur.
units.tr: Historians call these factions by other names, the Red Rose and the White Rose. For the men of York called themselves the White Rose, and the Lancastrians called themselves the Red Rose. How much evil these factions brought upon England can be seen above all from Philippe de Commynes. They were extinguished by Henry VII, who, having married Elizabeth, daughter of King Edward IV, joined the White Rose, that is the House of York, with the Red Rose, that is of Lancaster. Hence even today a double rose is seen among the insignia of the kings of England.

units.la: Cambria titulo Principatus Wal-liæ ad regnum Angliæ pervenit.
units.tr: Cambria came to the kingdom of England under the title of the Principality of Wales.

units.la: A. C. 1254. sub Heinrico III. Nam cùm Britanni[?] à Saxonibus pulsi o-mnem [?]mnem amisserunt regionem campe-strem & planam, profugerunt versus occidentem in altissimos montes, atque ibi natura locorum tuti & inexpugnabiles substiterunt, condito peculiari regnò quod Cambriam appellarunt. Ultimus eorum Rex fuit Cadvvalladher, cum quo omnem spem recuperandi Britanniam amiserunt. Post eum Cambria divisa fuit in Meridionalem & Septentrionalem, quarum utraque peculiares suos Reges habuit, quibus circa A. C. 1140 extincto Regum nomine Principes successerunt, quorum ultimus David Londini propter rebellionem securi percussus fuit. Actum temporis Cambria plene in po-testatem Regum Angliæ pervenit, quam Henricus III. Eduardo filio suo titulo Principatus Walliæ donavit, atq; ab eo tempore primogeniti filii Regum dicti fuerunt Principes Wallia. Nam antiqui Saxones pro-
units.tr: In AD 1254, under Henry III. For when the Britons, driven out by the Saxons, lost all the level and flat country, they fled westward into the highest mountains, and there, safe and impregnable by the nature of the place, they settled, founding a separate kingdom which they called Cambria. The last of their kings was Cadwallader, with whom they lost all hope of recovering Britain. After him Cambria was divided into Southern and Northern, each of which had its own kings. Around AD 1140, when the name of king had lapsed, princes succeeded them, the last of whom, David, was beheaded at London on account of rebellion. At length Cambria fully passed into the power of the kings of England, and Henry III gave it to his son Edward with the title of Prince of Wales; from that time the eldest sons of the kings were called Princes of Wales. For the ancient Saxons, on account of

units.la: pter lingvæ diversitatem appellarunt Cambros voce Germanicâ Wallos, quâ hodieqve utimur in denotandis hominibus barbaræ & nobis non intellectæ lingvæ.
units.tr: the diversity of language, called the Cambrians by the German word Wallos, which we still use today to denote people of a barbarous language that we do not understand.

units.la: Canon. Omnia regna Britannicæ sunt conjuncta.
units.tr: Canon. All the kingdoms of Britain are joined together.

units.la: A. C. 1603. post obitum Elisabethæ Jacobus IV Rex Scotiæ universam Britanniam i. e. 360 Insulas uno Imperio, quod ab orbe condito non fuerat factum, fuit complexus, atque abrogato Angliæ ac Scotiæ nomine universam Insulam Magnam Britanniam appellari voluit. Ei successit A. C. 1624 filius Carolus.
units.tr: In AD 1603, after the death of Elizabeth, James IV, king of Scotland, embraced the whole of Britain, that is 360 islands, in one empire, which had not been done since the world was created. Abolishing the names of England and Scotland, he wished the whole island to be called Great Britain. He was succeeded in AD 1624 by his son Charles.
The kingdoms of Britain were at some time divided again

units.la: quære-gna post bre[?] tò iterum fuere distracta, nunc tamen denuò conjuncta,
units.tr: after a short while, but now they are joined together once more.

units.la: A. C. 1649. Causa fuit Bellum Ci-vile inter Regem & Parlamentum, ex quo bello tria sunt consequta:
units.tr: A.D. 1649. The cause was the Civil War between the King and Parliament, and three things followed from this war:
1. The rebellion and defection of Ireland.

units.la: 3. Separatio Angliæ & Scotiæ; quarum illa titulum Reipublicæ assumsit: hæc Regem Carolum II suscepit; Sed eò paulò post armis Anglorum ejectò incertè fluctuavit usq; ad A. C. 1653 quò Generalis Olivarius Crom-welus publicis Comitiis Angliæ, Scotiæ & Hybernia Rerumpublicarum Protector salutatus est. Post hujus obitum Insularum dictarum incolæ A. C. 1660 & sequenti regiminis formam iterum mutarunt, & obtruncati Regis filium Carolum II ex Brabantia revocatum Regem constituerunt, qui adhuc hodie imperat.
units.tr: 3. The separation of England and Scotland; of these, the former assumed the title of Commonwealth, while the latter received King Charles II. But after he was driven out by the arms of the English, it wavered uncertainly until A.D. 1653, when the general Oliver Cromwell was hailed Protector of the Commonwealths of England, Scotland and Ireland by a public assembly. After his death, the inhabitants of the said islands changed the form of government again in A.D. 1660 and the following year, and recalled Charles II, son of the executed king, from Brabant and made him king, who still reigns today.
The Hunnic (language or peoples) is either Ugric, or Turkic, or Tartar.
The Huns founded the greatest empire.

units.la: Circa A. C. 400. universa Scy-thia nomine Hunnorum in Impe-rium Romanum irruit, Rege Balam-bere, cui successit Mundzuch Bende-gaz.
units.tr: Around A.D. 400 all Scythia, under the name of the Huns, invaded the Roman Empire, under King Balambere, who was succeeded by Mundzuch Bendegaz.
Attila was the first monarch of the Huns.

units.la: Cum Hunni Duces tantum & Principes hactenus habuissent A. C. 401 Attila omnium Hunnorum Impe-
units.tr: Although until then the Huns had had only dukes and princes, in A.D. 401 Attila was created emperor of all the Huns;

units.la: Imperator creatus fuit; qvi universam penè Europam, Germaniam, Pannoniam, Galliam & Italiam, partim in Societatem suam traxit, partim armorum terrore perculit; in-primis verò fortissimas gentes & Romano nomini infestissimas, Gothos, Gepidas, Longobardos, Herulos[?], in castra sua pertraxit. Inde propter uni-versalem vastitatem terrarum & internecionem dictus est: Flagellum Dei, & terror orbis. Victus est atroci prælio in campis Galliæ Catalannicis[?], & paulò post profluvio Sangvinis ex-tinctus universam Galliam terrore armorum suorum liberavit.
units.tr: he drew into his alliance almost the whole of Europe, Germany, Pannonia, Gaul and Italy, in part, and in part struck them with terror of his arms; above all, he drew into his camp the most valiant peoples and those most hostile to the Roman name, the Goths, Gepids, Lombards and Heruli[?]. From this he was called, because of the universal devastation of lands and slaughter, the Scourge of God, and the terror of the world. He was defeated in a fierce battle in the fields of Catalaunian[?] Gaul, and shortly afterwards, dying from a flow of blood, he freed all Gaul from the terror of his arms.

units.la: Hunni ex Europa in Asi-am repulsi.
units.tr: The Huns driven back from Europe into Asia.

units.la: Occasio fuit mors Attilæ; causa im-pulsivæ dissidium inter tres filios At-tilæ; tilæ; instrumentalis: plurimæ natio-nes potentes, Gothi, Gepidæ, Lon-gobardi, qvæ singulæ rebellarunt. Qvapropter Chaba, Attilæ filius natu major, cùm vidisset rem desperatam, reliqvias Hunnorum in Scythiam reduxit, paucis ultrò remanentibus, qvi, ne Hunnorum nomine suspecti essent, Siculos se appellarunt, & itahodieq; in Transylvania appel-lantur. Significat autem Siculorum nomen lingvâ Hunnicâ reliqvias.
units.tr: The occasion was the death of Attila; the impulsive cause was the dissension among Attila's three sons; the instrumental causes were the many powerful nations, the Goths, Gepids and Lombards, each of which rebelled. Therefore Chaba, the eldest of Attila's sons, seeing that the situation was hopeless, led the remnants of the Huns back into Scythia. A few remained behind of their own accord, and, so as not to be suspected of bearing the Hunnic name, they called themselves Siculi, and to this day they are called that in Transylvania. The name Siculorum means "remnants" in the Hunnic language.
